account: Guynn, Regis, Eckert, D'souza, Turbow, Westerman, Sperling and Lloyd are in Emory University School of Medicine's Division of Cardiology, Atlanta. They report on a 64-year-old man who had a bioprosthetic aortic valve replaced at 55. He had a month of intermittent palpitations and near-syncope. During symptoms he used his smartwatch's electrocardiogram (ECG) function. The watch's brand and model are unstated. The watch captured a 10-second single-lead ECG and reported a heart rate above 150 beats/min, warning him to speak to a doctor. The tracing showed wide complex tachycardia at 165 beats/min. On admission he was in sinus rhythm at 77 beats per minute. Telemetry and ECG then caught multiple episodes of monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, and he was admitted to intensive cardiac care. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) suggested scar or late myocarditis at the basal septum. An electrophysiology study found easily inducible ventricular tachycardia. Doctors implanted a secondary-prevention implantable defibrillator, and he was discharged on metoprolol, spironolactone and dapagliflozin. Three months later the defibrillator shocked him for ventricular tachycardia. Device interrogation showed pace-terminated episodes, some degenerating into ventricular fibrillation. Successful ablation below the aortic prosthesis followed, with no further ventricular tachycardia on serial interrogations. The report gives no event dates. The journal received it on 16 July 2024, so the smartwatch recording and the diagnosis took place before then. JACC: Case Reports published the report online on 12 March 2025. The authors write that ventricular tachycardia would have gone undiagnosed had the clinician not considered the smartwatch data. In November 2025 cardiologists at Lady Davis Carmel Medical Center in Haifa published a systematic review that cites this case and pools 20 published patients. They conclude that smartwatches may provide outpatient data that support timely diagnosis and therapy.

ai_role.statement: The device's contribution was recording a user-triggered single-lead ECG and issuing a generic high-heart-rate warning. It did not classify the rhythm as VT, which the authors say no wearable algorithm is validated to do. Clinicians read the QRS morphology on the smartwatch trace and on the 12-lead ECG, and made every treatment decision. The brand is unknown.

The authors are cardiologists at Lady Davis Carmel Medical Center in Haifa, declare no competing interests and have no tie to the Emory team; their review cites this case and pools 20 published patients, and they conclude that smartwatch data may support timely diagnosis.
evidence.quote: Smartwatches may provide valuable outpatient data that support timely diagnosis and appropriate therapy across diverse clinical scenarios.
evidence.title: Smartwatch-Based Detection of Ventricular Dysrhythmias: A Systematic Review of Literature

fields.account: Guynn, Regis, Eckert, D'souza, Turbow, Westerman, Sperling and Lloyd are in Emory University School of Medicine's Division of Cardiology, Atlanta. They report on a 64-year-old man who had a bioprosthetic aortic valve replaced at 55. He had a month of intermittent palpitations and near-syncope. During symptoms he used his smartwatch's electrocardiogram (ECG) function. The watch's brand and model are unstated. The watch captured a 10-second single-lead ECG and reported a heart rate above 150 beats/min, warning him to speak to a doctor. The tracing showed wide complex tachycardia at 165 beats/min. On admission he was in sinus rhythm at 77 beats per minute. Telemetry and ECG then caught multiple episodes of monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, and he was admitted to intensive cardiac care. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) suggested scar or late myocarditis at the basal septum. An electrophysiology study found easily inducible ventricular tachycardia. Doctors implanted a secondary-prevention implantable defibrillator, and he was discharged on metoprolol, spironolactone and dapagliflozin. Three months later the defibrillator shocked him for ventricular tachycardia. Device interrogation showed pace-terminated episodes, some degenerating into ventricular fibrillation. Successful ablation below the aortic prosthesis followed, with no further ventricular tachycardia on serial interrogations. The report gives no event dates. The journal received it on 16 July 2024, so the smartwatch recording and the diagnosis took place before then. JACC: Case Reports published the report online on 12 March 2025. The authors write that ventricular tachycardia would have gone undiagnosed had the clinician not considered the smartwatch data. In November 2025 cardiologists at Lady Davis Carmel Medical Center in Haifa published a systematic review that cites this case and pools 20 published patients. They conclude that smartwatches may provide outpatient data that support timely diagnosis and therapy.

echoes.setting: Three earlier published cases of VT diagnosed from a smartwatch recording, each leading to an electrophysiology study and ICD, ablation or both, as summarized in this report's discussion
echoes.source: Guynn N et al. (2025), JACC Case Rep 30(9):103273, discussion ('To date, there have only been 3 other reported cases of VT diagnosed by a smartwatch')

echoes.setting: Other published patients whose ventricular arrhythmias were captured by smartwatches, pooled in a systematic review of 20 patients from 18 articles up to May 2025

must_hold: The arrhythmia occurs while the wearer is able to trigger a recording (the watch has no continuous ECG)
The QRS morphology on a single lead is clear enough for a clinician to suspect VT and pursue confirmation
produced_by: A wearer who activates the watch's ECG recording during a transient symptomatic episode
A clinician who reviews the single-lead trace rather than dismissing consumer data
Access to telemetry, cardiac MRI, electrophysiology study, ICD implantation and ablation

purpose: Smartwatch ECG apps are built to record a single-lead trace and warn of high heart rates. Capturing the ventricular tachycardia during symptoms was that function. The authors note that no smartwatch algorithm is validated to detect ventricular tachycardia. Clinicians made the diagnosis from the trace.

ratings.reason: The smartwatch trace led to a diagnosis of ventricular tachycardia and to an implantable defibrillator, which later shocked him for ventricular tachycardia with episodes degenerating into ventricular fibrillation. A successful ablation followed, with no further ventricular tachycardia on serial interrogations. A life-threatening arrhythmia was diagnosed and resolved in time.
